description: I am an energetic elementary school student and space enthusiast who dreams of exploring the cosmos! Proving that we are never too young to tackle big galactic ideas, I bring a new perspective, limitless curiosity, and a deep love for astronomy to this year's NASA International Space Apps Challenge. I am completely fascinated by planets, stars, space, and black holes. Guided by this excitement for space exploration, I am here to learn, create, and show that great innovations can start at any age
summary: Space Exploration 2026 is a free web game where kids plan a space mission to the Moon, Mars, Jupiter's moons and explore Jupiter or a Mystery Planet. Players pick a landing site, pack a rocket within limits on coins, mass and power, test the plan with a worst-case simulator, then watch the mission play out as surprise events hit, such as dust storms, solar flares and radiation. It answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge: players design, manage and simulate a full mission, and the game explains why each choice helped or hurt. It matters because it teaches the real trade-offs engineers face, in words an 8-year-old can follow, and every option can win with the right thinking.
details:
What it does: four missions, easiest to hardest. Moon (survive the 14-day lunar night), Mars (water, air and food for 4 astronauts for a year), Jupiter (a robot that must survive radiation and send data home, with three orbit choices), and a Mystery Planet (read telescope clues and decide if life is possible).

How it works: every mission has 4 rounds. Mission academy explains the game and roles you play. Space Arli - a bot guides the player through the game as needed. Following are the different stages of the game - 1) Research: pick a site (and an orbit on Jupiter). 2) Prepare: a shop where parts cost coins, mass and power; the rocket must carry the payload; a "Ready to launch?" checklist and a Simulate button test the plan in the worst case. 3) Explore: random events. 4) Sustain: an animated story that stops only when the player must decide, such as switching machines off when power runs short. The score is out of 100 (60 to pass), with tips on what to try next and a mission report.

Benefits: teaches budgets, mass, power, life support, communications, data and orbits through play. Includes team mode for 1–4 players with roles (Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Officer, Life Support & Comms), two objectives per planet, a sandbox mode, a Clues button, a glossary and read-aloud.

What we hope to achieve: help kids think like mission engineers: there is rarely one perfect answer, test before you launch, and every choice has a cost.

Tools: one HTML file (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), no libraries. Fonts: Fredoka and Nunito (Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License). Hosted on GitHub Pages. Tested with Playwright. Code written with help from Claude (AI). License: MIT.
